newsitem.title: UK: World woolgrowers suffered tough season in 1995/96.
newsitem.headline: World woolgrowers suffered tough season in 1995/96.

text.p: The world's wool trade was hit by plummeting prices, declining demand and the failure of a falling sheep population to limit the damage, according to the International Wool Textile Organisation (IWTO).
"The 1995-6 season proved critical for the wool industry, with many (participants) struggling for survival," the body, known as the industry's parliament, said in its annual statistical review.
Wool values fell across most microns despite the lowest global availability for more than twenty years, the report said.
"Prices have fallen to unprofitable levels for woolgrowers so that at primary production level, ground has been lost to grains, cattle and forestry in particular," it said.

Finest microns led the general decline in apparel wool prices with 19-microns losing 37 percent of their value over the season, 20-microns 34 percent and 21-micron wool falling 25 percent. Coarser crossbred wool prices fell about ten percent.
Consumption also reached the lowest level since the 1970s, dropping seven percent to 1.479 million tonnes clean wool against available supplies of about 1.65 million tonnes.
The IWTO ascribed the fall in wool usage to trade restrictions in China, structural changes within the Japanese textile industry, slow global economic growth and high unemployment in Europe.
The season also saw a six percent reduction in the size of the world clip to around 1.47 million tonnes clean wool, due largely to falling output in Australia, Russia and New Zealand.
Australia's share of world output fell six percent to 30.4 percent as poor returns encouraged woolgrowers to change to arable farming and drought conditions reduced the overall sheep population.

New Zealand's contribution fell 0.1 percent to 13.6 percent as sheep numbers and average fleece weights declined due to mixed growing conditions and the ongoing trend for woolgrowers to switch to cattle and lumber production.

The report estimated the clip size in the main CIS wool regions (Russia, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan) at a collective 129,000 tonnes clean, a 24 percent decline in the year, leaving it with 8.8 percent of world production.
The sheep population is said to have been slashed by high local slaughter rates and live sheep exports.

But the CIS turned from a net importer to become the world's fourth biggest wool exporter, as defence cuts in Russia drastically reduced domestic production of military uniforms, and surplus stock was hived off to China.
China boosted production by around one percent to between 70,000 and 80,000 tonnes.

Although it leapfrogged Russia to become the world's third biggest producer after Australia and New Zealand, China remained the world's biggest wool importer, buying around twice the amount of second-placed rival Italy.
Fifth-placed Uruguay's wool output dropped six percent to 56,000 tonnes clean as survival rates and fleece weights were scythed by extreme weather conditions.
Argentinian production fell nine percent to 43,000 tonnes clean, the lowest level for almost twenty-five years, as the switch to meat and grain production accelerated.
South African output was unchanged at around 39,000 tonnes clean.
